rv.q: A tough, troubling, revealing play: proof again that the stage has become an excellent place to grapple, collectively, with our fraught and freighted times and to help us listen better to our own responses.
It’s an elegant, essential provocation from a singular writer whose voice – needling, sly, hyper-aware – demands attention.
Harris’s play is full of a sharp satirical intelligence that makes the right words fall from the wrong mouths, and resists pat conclusions.
In the end I felt ‘Slave Play’ is really made by its dynamite final scene, which solely features Wahington’s Kaneisha and Harington’s Jim.
It might be flawed but it is charismatic, needling theatre.
Walking away from this work unaffected or free from a brain-buzz of complexities is simply not an option.
Crucially, this couple give a diagrammatic play a sudden human pulse.
It’s never boring, but it’s only the satirical side that works.
It fizzes with provocative ideas, but it is also uneven and, at more than two hours without interval, excessively baggy.
All told, it actually feels like a valuable work-in-progress about America’s vexed race relations.
Jeremy O Harris’s play comes across as the sort of ideas-led piece that would stimulate over an hour but has instead unwisely swollen to two hours.
But I couldn’t help but feel that the play fails at what it sets out to do.
Suffice to say, it is a loveless piece of work, from which many people, of all ethnicities, may wish in retrospect that they too had been excluded.
It’s a gripping and unapologetically challenging play with hard-to-stomach subject matter.
There is undoubtedly a pervading artificiality to the single-lens perspective through which the failures of the biracial relationships being examined are perceived.
For a play that wears controversy as a badge of honour the last thing I expected to feel was slightly bored.
This is an uneven play that feels like it is doing more damage than good to race relations.
Slave Play is too obsessed with conceptual naval gazing to the extent that it forgets that its characters are human beings.
The play seems to reinforce the caricatures it sets out to diminish.
None of the sections is believable.
It’s funny, clever and undoubtedly challenging.
It is enough to say bravely, wittily, with superb acting and not a little discomfort.
With the programme’s cover explicitly symbolising vagina, Slave Play feels bizarrely disconnected from female desire.

cn.t: Provocative drama about race and sexuality divides critics, with praise for its bold ideas and performances but criticism for overlong therapy scenes and reliance on shock value over substance.
